intro: A tenth grader freezes on a chemistry quiz because of one word, then remembers a scrap of Latin from English class and works the word out. Two farmers rebuild a stone wall in a poem, and by the last line the wall is no longer only a wall. Both moments come from the same fact about language: words are not sealed boxes. They are built from parts that travel between subjects, and they can carry a second meaning that the writer never states out loud.

This unit teaches two skills that separate readers who cope from readers who understand. The first is taking a word apart: reading the context around it, seeing the root inside it, tracing where it came from, noticing when a science word or a history word is an ordinary word in disguise, and knowing which reference tool answers which question. The second is reading a figure of speech: metaphor, symbol, allegory, irony, paradox, allusion and euphemism, each a way of saying one thing and meaning another.

By the end you will be able to meet an unfamiliar word in any class and make a defensible guess, choose the exact word when you write, and explain what a figure of speech does to the meaning and tone of a text, with evidence from the words on the page. That last skill is what every literature essay in high school and college is asking for.
bigQuestion: How do readers and writers get more meaning out of a word than its dictionary definition holds?

test.q: The trail was arduous, so steep that we rested every ten minutes. What kind of context clue explains arduous?
choices: A restatement that describes the difficulty
test.why: The clause after the comma restates arduous by describing how hard the trail was.

test.q: Which word shares a root with predict and contradict?
test.why: Dict means say; a dictionary is a book of sayings and their meanings.

test.q: What does the prefix in- mean in the word inflammable?
test.why: Inflammable means able to burst into flame; here in- means into, not not.

test.q: Which suffix turns a word into a noun?
test.why: Kindness and darkness are nouns; -ly makes adverbs, -ize verbs, -ous adjectives.

test.q: Which word's history shows a meaning rising from humble to honored?
test.why: Knight once meant a boy or servant and rose to a title of honor.

test.q: A Spanish-speaking student reads that a character actually left. Which is true?
choices: Actually is a false cognate of actualmente and here means in fact, not currently
Actually means currently, as in Spanish
test.why: Spanish actualmente means currently; English actually means in fact, so the pair is a false cognate.

choices: It probably means the space something takes up, and the sentence will confirm this

test.q: Which sentence uses the most precise word?
choices: The dog went across the yard.
The dog moved across the yard.
The dog was in the yard.
The dog limped across the yard.
test.why: Limped tells the reader how the dog moved and hints that it was hurt; the others say almost nothing.

test.why: Every character and event lines up with a meaning outside the story, which makes it allegory.

Accept it as a technical term with no other meaning
Treat it as a metaphor about money
Treat it as an allusion to a war
test.why: Euphemisms are tested by translating them; this one exists to soften a hard fact.

The poet uses a metaphor in line three.
The poet uses imagery to make the poem interesting.
By calling the neighbor an old-stone savage, the speaker makes him seem stuck in the dark and sounds a little superior himself.
test.why: It names the figure, unpacks the vehicle and states the effect on tone.

write.prompt: Frost's speaker mocks the wall but rebuilds it every spring. Make a claim about what Mending Wall says about walls between people, and support it with the poem's figurative language: the symbol of the wall, the repeated line Good fences make good neighbors, and the image of the neighbor as an old-stone savage armed.
tips: State one clear claim in a sentence a thoughtful reader could disagree with.
Use at least two figures from the poem as evidence, quoting the exact words and naming the kind of figure.
For each figure, do the three moves: name it, unpack the vehicle or symbol, and state its effect on tone.
Deal with the other side: the speaker helps rebuild the wall. What does that do to your claim?
Keep your own figures of speech to one at most; let the poem supply the poetry and your sentences supply the clarity.

title: Words and Structure

chapters.title: Context Clues and Word Parts
chapters.bigQuestion: When you meet a word you have never seen, what can the sentence around it and the pieces inside it tell you?

story.title: The Word That Flew Away From the Center
story.kicker: A tenth grader is stuck on a chemistry quiz until a line of Latin from English class floats back to her.
paragraphs: Marisol had studied the chapter. She knew how to separate salt from sand and how to filter a cloudy liquid. Then question seven asked what a centrifuge does to a mixture of blood cells and plasma. She had never heard the word. Her pencil stopped. Twenty minutes were left, and she could feel the clock more than she could read the question.

She did what she had been taught to do with a stranger of a word. She looked at the pieces. The first part, centri, looked like center. She knew that one from centimeter and from the center of a circle. The second part, fuge, did not look like anything at all. Or did it? A memory from English class nudged her.

Two weeks earlier, her English teacher had written a scrap of Latin on the board from the Roman poet Virgil: fugit irreparabile tempus. Time flees, and it cannot be brought back. The class had laughed because he said it while stealing a glance at the clock. Fugit meant flees. Fuge, then, might mean flee or fly away from. A centrifuge would be something that makes things fly away from the center.

That was enough to picture it. A machine spins a tube very fast. The heavier parts of the mixture get thrown outward, away from the center, toward the bottom of the tube. The lighter liquid stays on top. Marisol wrote that the centrifuge spins the blood so the cells settle out from the plasma. She got the point, and she got something better than the point.

The word had not been a stranger after all. It was a relative of fugitive, a person who flees, and of refuge, a place you flee to. It shared a root with a two-thousand-year-old poem. Words are built from parts, and the parts travel. Once you can see them, a new word in chemistry or history or math is often an old word wearing a lab coat.
story.think: Think of a word you learned in one class that later helped you understand a word in a completely different class. What part of the word carried the meaning across?

sections.title: Reading the Clues Around a Word

lessons.title: Five Kinds of Context Clues
lessons.mainIdea: Writers often plant the meaning of a hard word nearby, and there are five common places to look for it.
reading: Read this sentence. The council's decision was met with derision, and people laughed openly at the plan for weeks. You may not know *derision*. But the sentence tells you. People laughed openly. Derision means scornful laughter or mockery. The writer did not stop to define the word. The writer simply put its meaning next door. That is a *context clue*, a hint in the surrounding words that points to what a word means.

There are five kinds you will meet again and again. A definition clue states the meaning outright: A peninsula, which is land surrounded by water on three sides, juts into the lake. An example clue lists members of the group: Amphibians, such as frogs, toads and salamanders, live both in water and on land. A synonym clue restates the idea in an easier word: The old bridge was precarious, so shaky that no truck would cross it. A contrast clue tells you what the word is not: Unlike her talkative brother, Nia was reticent at dinner. A cause-and-effect clue shows what the word leads to: Because the medicine was potent, one small dose stopped the pain.

Notice the signal words. Which is, such as, or, unlike, because, so. These small words are flags that a clue is nearby. When you hit a hard word, do not reread the word ten times. Read the whole sentence, then the sentence before and after it, and hunt for a flag. Then make a guess and test it. Put your guess in place of the word and read the sentence again. If it still makes sense, keep going.

One warning. Context gives you a working meaning, not always the exact one. From the first sentence you can tell derision is a kind of mocking. You could not tell from context alone that it comes from a Latin word meaning to laugh at. For a quiz, a working meaning is usually enough. For a word you will need again, check a dictionary later and write it down.

words.d: a hint in the words around an unfamiliar word that points to its meaning
scornful laughter; mocking someone or something as ridiculous
quiet; not willing to speak much or reveal your thoughts
unstable; likely to fall or fail

look.title: One Sentence, Five Flags
look.text: The storm left the road impassable, so blocked with fallen trees that even the plow, unlike the small emergency truck, had to turn back, because nothing wider than a bicycle could get through.
look.prompt: Find every signal word in this sentence. Which clues tell you what impassable means, and which one is the strongest? Explain in one sentence.

check.q: In the sentence about the council, what tells the reader that derision means mockery?
check.why: The clause after the comma describes people laughing at the plan, which restates what derision means.

check.q: Which sentence uses a contrast clue?
choices: Amphibians, such as frogs, live in water and on land.
A peninsula, which is land surrounded by water on three sides, juts out.
Unlike her talkative brother, Nia was reticent.
Because the medicine was potent, one dose worked.
check.why: The word unlike signals that reticent is the opposite of talkative.

check.q: What is the best way to test a guess about a word's meaning?
choices: Reread the word until it looks familiar
Skip the sentence and keep reading
Ask whether the word looks like Spanish
Put the guess in the word's place and reread the sentence
check.why: If the sentence still makes sense with your guess substituted, the guess is probably close.

lessons.title: When the Clue Is Far Away
lessons.mainIdea: Sometimes no single sentence explains a word, and you must gather hints from the whole paragraph or passage.
reading: Here is a paragraph with no easy flags. The village had been in a drought for three summers. The wells were dry. Farmers sold their animals because there was nothing to feed them. Children were sent to cousins in the city. When the rain finally came, people stood in the road and let it soak their clothes, and some of them wept. You are not told what *drought* means in the sentence where it appears. But every sentence after it is evidence. Dry wells, nothing to feed the animals, people weeping in the rain. A drought is a long stretch without rain. The paragraph taught you by showing the effects.

This is *inference*, a conclusion you draw from clues that add up. Reading for a word this way is like being a detective. You ask, what is the situation here? What would have to be true for these details to make sense? Then you name it. The same skill works on a page of history or a science article. If a text keeps describing a thing without defining it, the description is the definition.

There is a second far-away clue: the topic itself. If you are reading about volcanoes and meet the word *magma*, the topic narrows the possibilities before you read another word. It is something to do with volcanoes, probably the hot melted rock, since the passage talks about heat and pressure underground. Headings, pictures, captions and the title all shrink the field. Use them before you get stuck, not after.

One more tool is your own experience. The paragraph about the drought works because you know what dry wells and hungry animals mean. When a passage is about something you have lived, trust what you know. When it is about something far from your life, slow down and lean harder on the text. Good readers do both, and they notice which one they are doing.

words.d: a conclusion you reach by putting clues together, not something the text states directly
a long period with little or no rain
hot melted rock beneath the surface of the earth

look.title: A Paragraph That Never Defines Its Word
look.text: Devon was the most gregarious kid on the block. He knew every neighbor's name and their dog's name. At parties he moved from group to group and never ate alone. When the family moved, the hardest part for him was a lunchroom where nobody knew him yet.
look.prompt: What does gregarious mean? List the three details that told you, and explain which one you used first.

check.q: How does the drought paragraph teach the meaning of drought?
choices: It gives a dictionary definition in parentheses
It shows the effects of a drought in several sentences
It uses the signal word because
It gives a synonym after a comma
check.why: Dry wells, starving animals and joy at the rain add up to a long time without rain.

check.q: What kind of clue is the topic of a passage?
choices: A far-away clue that narrows what a word could mean
check.why: Knowing the passage is about volcanoes limits what magma is likely to mean before you read the sentence.

check.q: When should a reader lean hardest on the text rather than on personal experience?
choices: When the topic is far from the reader's own life
When the word has a Latin root
check.why: Experience helps most with familiar situations; unfamiliar ones require closer attention to the text's details.

lessons.title: Roots That Carry Meaning
lessons.mainIdea: A few dozen Latin and Greek roots appear in thousands of academic words, and knowing the root gives you a foothold.
reading: Look at these words: transport, portable, export, import, report, support, deport. Seven words, one shared piece. Port comes from the Latin portare, to carry. Transport is to carry across. Portable means it can be carried. Export is to carry out of a country. Once you see port, you can make a fair guess at any word that contains it. That shared piece is a *root*, the part of a word that holds its core meaning.

Academic words lean heavily on a small set of roots. Dict means say: predict, contradict, verdict, dictate, dictionary, diction. Spect means look: inspect, spectator, perspective, respect, spectacle, suspect. Scrib or script means write: describe, manuscript, prescription, scribble, transcript. Bene means good or well: benefit, benevolent, benefactor, benign. Greek gives us graph for writing, bio for life, chron for time, and tele for far. A telegraph writes at a distance. A chronology is the order of events in time.

The root is a foothold, not the whole climb. Verdict is a true saying, which is what a jury gives. But respect does not mean look again in ordinary use; it has drifted to mean regard someone highly. The root gets you close. The sentence takes you the rest of the way. So use both. Ask what the root suggests, then check that meaning against the context. When the two agree, you can be confident.

Start noticing roots in your other classes. In biology, a *biography* of a cell is not on the test, but biology, biome, antibiotic and symbiosis are, and bio is in every one. In history, a chronicle and an anachronism both hold chron. A student who knows twenty roots is not memorizing twenty words. She is holding a key to several hundred.

words.d: the part of a word that carries its basic meaning, often from Latin or Greek
the decision a jury announces; literally a true saying
the order in which events happened in time
the written story of a real person's life

look.title: Word Families Built on One Root
look.cite: counted for this lesson from the word lists in the reading
look.prompt: These are only the words listed here; each family is really larger. Add two more words to any family, and say what the root contributes to each.

check.q: What does the root port mean in transport, export and portable?
check.why: Port comes from the Latin portare, to carry; transport is to carry across.

check.q: Which word contains a root meaning to look?
check.why: Spect means look; a spectator is someone who watches.

check.q: Why does the lesson call a root a foothold and not the whole climb?
choices: Because roots are only found in science words
Because some words have drifted from their root meaning and context must confirm the guess
Because Greek roots are harder than Latin roots
Because most English words have no root
check.why: Respect no longer means look again; the root gets you close, and the sentence finishes the job.

lessons.title: Prefixes and Suffixes at Work
lessons.mainIdea: A prefix changes a word's meaning at the front, and a suffix often changes its job in the sentence at the back.
reading: Take the root just, meaning fair. Add un at the front and you get unjust, the opposite. Add ice at the back and you get justice, a noun. Add ify and you get justify, a verb. Add ly and you get justly, an adverb. The root never changed. The pieces stuck on either side did all the work. A piece added to the front is a *prefix*. A piece added to the end is a *suffix*. Together with roots, these are the building blocks of most long words.

Prefixes mostly change meaning. Un, in, non and dis make a word negative: unclear, invisible, nonsense, dishonest. The prefix in has costumes: it becomes im before p or m (impossible, immature), il before l (illegal) and ir before r (irregular). Re means again or back: rewrite, return. Pre means before: preview, predict. Sub means under: submarine, subway. Trans means across: transport, translate. Number prefixes count: mono for one, bi for two, tri for three, as in monorail, bicycle, triangle.

Suffixes mostly change a word's part of speech. Tion, ment, ness and ity make nouns: action, movement, kindness, clarity. Ize and ify make verbs: realize, simplify. Ous, ful, less and able make adjectives: dangerous, hopeful, careless, readable. Ly makes adverbs: quickly. Once you know this, you can tell what a word is doing even when you are unsure what it means. If a word ends in ness, it is a thing, a quality. If it ends in ize, someone is doing something.

A caution about in. It does not always mean not. Sometimes it means in or into. *Inflammable* does not mean unable to burn. It means able to burst into flame, from the Latin inflammare, to set on fire. So many people misread it that safety labels now say flammable instead. When a prefix could go two ways, let the context decide. A word on a gas can that warns you is not telling you the gas is safe.

words.d: a word part added to the front of a word that changes its meaning, such as un- or pre-
a word part added to the end of a word that often changes its part of speech, such as -ness or -ly
able to catch fire easily; the same meaning as flammable

look.title: Build a Word Family
look.text: Start with the root act. Now add pieces: react, action, active, actively, activate, inactive, interaction, reactivation. Each piece either pushes the meaning or changes the word's job.
look.prompt: Sort the eight words into nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs. Then explain what re, inter and in each do to the meaning.

check.q: Which of these changes a word's part of speech most often?
check.why: Suffixes like -tion, -ize and -ly turn words into nouns, verbs and adverbs.

check.q: What does inflammable mean?
check.why: Here in- means into, not not; inflammable and flammable mean the same thing.

check.q: Why does the prefix in- appear as im- in impossible?
choices: Because impossible is a Greek word
Because in- always becomes im- in adjectives
Because in- changes its spelling before p or m
check.why: The prefix adapts to the sound that follows it: im- before p or m, il- before l, ir- before r.

lessons.title: How Words Change Meaning
lessons.mainIdea: Words drift over centuries, and knowing where a word came from helps you remember it and use it well.
reading: Six hundred years ago, calling someone nice was an insult. Nice came from the Latin nescius, which means ignorant, not knowing. Over centuries it softened from foolish to fussy to pleasant. Silly once meant blessed and happy in Old English. Awful once meant full of awe, the feeling you have before something enormous, like a storm or a mountain. Now it just means very bad. The study of where words come from and how they have changed is *etymology*.

Some words keep a picture inside them. Muscle comes from the Latin musculus, little mouse, because a muscle moving under the skin looked like a small mouse running. Companion comes from com, with, and panis, bread: a companion is someone you share bread with. *Decimate* comes from a brutal Roman army punishment in which one soldier in every ten was killed. Today it usually means to destroy a large part of something, and most dictionaries accept that use, though a few careful writers still object.

Meaning drifts in predictable directions. Words narrow: meat once meant any food, now only animal flesh. Words widen: a holiday was once a holy day, now any day off. Words rise: knight once meant a boy or servant. Words fall: villain once meant a farm worker, then a low person, then a criminal. Knowing the direction of the drift helps you read older texts. When a character in a two-hundred-year-old novel is called nice, do not assume it is praise.

Etymology is also a memory tool. A word you know the story of is a word you keep. Centrifuge stays because of Virgil. Companion stays because of bread. When you look up a new word, glance at the origin line in the dictionary entry. It is usually in brackets, and it is often the most interesting part.

words.d: the history of a word: where it came from and how its form and meaning changed
originally to kill one in ten; now, to destroy a large part of something
a feeling of wonder mixed with fear or respect before something vast

look.title: Virgil on Time
look.text: In the Georgics, the Roman poet Virgil writes that meanwhile time flees, time that cannot be recovered. The Latin word for flees is fugit, and it survives in the English words fugitive, refuge and centrifuge.
look.prompt: Using what fugit means, explain what a refuge is and what a fugitive is. How does the root connect the two words?

check.q: What did nice originally mean?
check.why: Nice comes from the Latin nescius, not knowing; it took centuries to soften into praise.

check.q: Which is an example of a word's meaning narrowing over time?
choices: Meat, once any food, now animal flesh
Holiday, once a holy day, now any day off
Villain, once a farm worker, now a criminal
Knight, once a servant, now a title of honor
check.why: Meat went from a wide meaning to a narrow one; holiday widened, villain fell, knight rose.

check.q: Why does the lesson call etymology a memory tool?
choices: Because a word with a story behind it is easier to remember
Because etymology tells you how to pronounce a word
check.why: Muscle as a little mouse and companion as bread-sharer stick because they carry a picture.

lessons.title: Cognates Across Languages
lessons.mainIdea: If you speak Spanish or another language built from Latin, thousands of English academic words are already half yours.
reading: If you read Spanish, look at these English words: important, family, animal, nation, analysis, evidence, hypothesis. Now look at their Spanish twins: importante, familia, animal, nación, análisis, evidencia, hipótesis. They look alike because they are alike. They descend from the same Latin or Greek parent. Words like these are *cognates*, relatives across languages. For a student who reads Spanish, Portuguese, French or Italian, the hardest words in an English textbook are often the easiest, because those are the Latin ones.

This is not a small advantage. Everyday English is mostly Germanic: house, bread, run, think. But the vocabulary of science, law, medicine and school is largely Latin and Greek: photosynthesis, constitution, circulation, geometry. A Spanish speaker who feels behind in English conversation may be ahead in English chemistry. The trick is to notice the cognate and trust it. Fotosíntesis, constitución, circulación, geometría.

But be careful of the *false cognate*, a word that looks like a twin and is not. In Spanish, embarazada means pregnant, not embarrassed. Actual means current, so actualmente means currently, not actually. Éxito means success, not exit. Librería means bookstore, not library. Sensible means sensitive. These traps are few compared with the thousands of true cognates, but they are worth a list of their own. When a cognate makes a sentence strange, check it.

If you speak a language that is not built from Latin, such as Polish, Arabic, Chinese, Tagalog or Urdu, cognates will be fewer, but not zero. Many languages borrowed the same Greek and Latin science words. And the roots in the last lessons work for everyone, whatever your first language. Illinois classrooms hold speakers of well over a hundred languages. Every one of those students brings a word bank into the room. Use yours.

words.d: a word in one language that shares an origin and a similar form with a word in another language
a word that looks like a relative in another language but means something different
belonging to the family of languages that includes English, German and Dutch

look.title: Two Sentences, One Trap
look.text: A student writes in an English essay: The actual president of the club is Rosa, and the concert was a big exit. A reader is confused. The student meant the current president and a big success.
look.prompt: Which two Spanish false cognates caused the confusion? Rewrite the sentence in clear English, then name two true cognates the student could rely on instead.

check.q: Why are academic English words often easy for Spanish readers?
choices: Because Spanish has no academic words
Because most academic English words come from Latin and Greek, as Spanish does
Because academic words are shorter in English
check.why: School and science vocabulary in English is largely Latin and Greek, the same sources as Spanish.

check.q: What does the Spanish word éxito mean?
check.why: Éxito is a false cognate; it means success, not exit.

check.q: What should a reader do when a cognate makes a sentence sound strange?
choices: Assume the writer made a spelling mistake
Translate the whole sentence word by word
Check whether it is a false cognate
check.why: A strange result is the warning sign of a false cognate; a quick check settles it.

sections.title: Words at Work in Each Subject

lessons.title: Science Words With Everyday Twins
lessons.mainIdea: Many science terms are ordinary words with a precise second meaning, and you must switch meanings when you switch rooms.
reading: In the hallway, a solution is the answer to a problem. In chemistry, a *solution* is a mixture in which one substance is dissolved evenly in another, like salt in water. Same spelling, different word. A base in the hallway is where a runner stands. In chemistry it is a substance that accepts hydrogen ions, the opposite of an acid. Volume on your phone means loudness. Volume in a lab means how much space something takes up. These are *domain-specific* words: words with a special meaning inside one field of study.

The trouble is that the everyday meaning is louder in your head. When a lab question says find the volume of the gas, a tired reader may think of sound and freeze. The fix is to expect the switch. In a science text, assume an ordinary word means its science meaning until proven otherwise. Then check. Does volume of the gas make sense as loudness? No. As space? Yes. Read on.

Watch for this pattern in physics and biology too. Work in physics is force times distance, not homework. Power is how fast work is done. A conductor carries electricity, not a train ticket. In biology, a cell is not a phone or a prison room, a tissue is not for your nose, and a culture is bacteria growing in a dish. Each field is its own room with its own dictionary hanging on the wall.

Here is a practical habit. When your science textbook prints a word in bold, that is a signal that the ordinary meaning is not the one you need. Write the science meaning next to the everyday one in your notes. Solution: answer, or a dissolved mixture. Seeing both side by side stops the two from blurring together at test time.

words.d: belonging to one field of study, with a meaning that is precise inside that field
in chemistry, a uniform mixture in which one substance is dissolved in another
in physics, a material that lets electricity or heat pass through it easily

look.title: Three Sentences, One Word
look.text: 1. Turn down the volume; the baby is asleep. 2. The volume of the balloon doubled when it warmed up. 3. The library has the second volume of the encyclopedia.
look.prompt: Give the meaning of volume in each sentence. Which clues told you which meaning applied? Which one belongs to science?

check.q: What is a solution in chemistry?
choices: A mixture in which one substance is dissolved evenly in another
A liquid that has been boiled
check.why: The chemistry meaning is a uniform dissolved mixture, like salt in water.

check.q: What does the lesson advise about ordinary words in a science text?
choices: Assume the science meaning first, then check
Look every one up in a thesaurus
check.why: In a science room, expect the science meaning and confirm it with the sentence.

check.q: In physics, what does work mean?
choices: Any activity done in a lab
check.why: Physics defines work precisely as force applied over a distance.

lessons.title: History and Math Words
lessons.mainIdea: History and math also borrow ordinary words and sharpen them, so read the subject's meaning, not the street meaning.
reading: A history book says the colonists demanded representation. In the cafeteria, a party is a celebration. In history, a *party* is an organized political group, like the Democratic and Republican parties. A cabinet is not for dishes; it is the group of advisers who head a president's departments. A bill is not what you pay; it is a proposed law. Depression can be a sad mood, a low spot in the ground, or the Great Depression, the economic collapse that began in 1929. Revolution can mean one spin of a wheel or the overthrow of a government.

Math is even stricter. The *mean* of a set of numbers is their average, nothing to do with being unkind. A product is what you get when you multiply. A radical is the root sign, not a rebel. Odd numbers are not strange. A table is a grid of values. A function pairs each input with exactly one output. In math, a word means one thing only, and the whole subject depends on that. If a problem says find the product of 6 and 4, the answer is 24, not a thing you buy.

How do you tell which meaning is on the page? The same way as in science: expect the subject's meaning, then confirm it. But history adds a twist. Historical texts often use words in their older senses, because the writers lived then. In a document from 1776, a state may mean a nation, and awful may still mean awe-inspiring. Reading history well means reading with the etymology lesson in one hand.

One last group is the *technical* word that never appears outside its subject: integer, hypotenuse, feudalism, tariff. These are honest strangers. Nobody expects you to know them from the street. They are always defined somewhere in the chapter, usually near the first time they appear. Find that spot, and copy the definition in your own words.

words.d: in history and government, an organized group that seeks to win elections and hold power
in math, the average: the sum of the values divided by how many there are
belonging to a specialized field and rarely used outside it

look.title: A Word Doing Two Jobs
look.text: The mean temperature in Chicago last week was 41 degrees. That is not a mean thing to say; it is just the average. Find the product of the two means and you will have a number, not a thing you can buy.
look.prompt: Identify each math word in the passage and give its everyday meaning and its math meaning. Then write a sentence of your own that uses one word both ways.

check.q: In history, what is a bill?
check.why: A bill is a draft of a law that a legislature debates and may pass.

check.q: What is the product of 5 and 3?
check.why: Product means the result of multiplying: 5 times 3 is 15.

check.q: Why must you read older historical documents with etymology in mind?
choices: Because they are written in Latin
Because the writers used words in senses common in their own time
Because older documents have no context clues
check.why: State could mean nation and awful could mean awe-inspiring in 1776; meanings have drifted since.

lessons.title: Choosing the Exact Word
lessons.mainIdea: Near-synonyms are not equal, and the precise word tells the reader more in less space.
reading: He walked across the room. Now try: he strolled, he trudged, he marched, he crept, he staggered. Every one means he moved on foot from one side to the other. But strolled says relaxed. Trudged says tired and heavy. Marched says purpose and maybe anger. Crept says he did not want to be heard. Staggered says hurt or dizzy. A single verb did the work of a whole sentence of description. That is *precision*: choosing the word whose meaning fits exactly.

Words that mean almost the same thing carry different shades. Thin, slender, skinny and gaunt all describe a narrow body. Slender is admiring. Skinny is a little rude. Gaunt suggests illness or hunger. The neutral core meaning is the word's *denotation*. The feeling and the suggestion attached to it is its *connotation*. Precise writers choose for both. If you write that a politician is stubborn, you have judged. If you write determined, you have praised. Same behavior, different word, different verdict.

Vague words hide meaning. Nice, good, bad, thing, stuff, very and a lot say almost nothing. The party was good tells the reader nothing about the party. The party was loud, crowded and over by ten tells the reader everything. When you revise, hunt for the vague words and ask what you actually mean. Usually there is a sharper word waiting.

Precision also matters when you read. When a poet chooses gaunt and not thin, or a scientist writes accelerate and not speed up, the choice is a clue. Ask why this word and not the easier one. In an essay about a text, quoting the exact word and explaining its shade is one of the best moves you can make.

words.d: choosing the word whose meaning fits exactly, not just approximately
the plain dictionary meaning of a word
the feelings and associations a word carries beyond its plain meaning
very thin in a way that suggests hunger or illness

look.title: One Sentence, Six Verbs
look.text: The coach said, Sit down. The coach snapped, Sit down. The coach murmured, Sit down. The coach begged, Sit down. The coach growled, Sit down. The coach sighed, Sit down.
look.prompt: Describe the coach's mood in each version using one adjective. Which verb would you choose if the team had just lost by thirty points, and why?

check.q: Which verb suggests that a person is tired and moving heavily?
check.why: Trudged carries the connotation of slow, heavy, weary walking.

check.q: What is the connotation of a word?
choices: The feelings and suggestions it carries
check.why: Denotation is the plain meaning; connotation is the shade of feeling attached.

check.q: Why does the lesson call nice, good and stuff vague words?
choices: Because they tell the reader almost nothing specific
Because they cannot be used in essays
check.why: The party was good gives no detail; loud, crowded and over by ten paints the scene.

lessons.title: Three Reference Tools
lessons.mainIdea: A dictionary, a thesaurus and an etymology dictionary answer three different questions, and the skill is knowing which to open.
reading: You meet the word candid in a novel. Open a *dictionary*. The entry gives you the spelling, how to say it, its part of speech (adjective), its meanings in order, and often a sample sentence: candid, truthful and straightforward, not hiding anything. Most entries also give a short origin in brackets: from Latin candidus, white or pure. The dictionary is the tool for a word you have met and do not know. Print or online, it answers what does this mean and how is it used.

Now you are writing, and you have used the word said six times. Open a *thesaurus*. It lists words with related meanings: stated, remarked, muttered, declared, announced. But the thesaurus does not explain the shades. Muttered and declared are not interchangeable. So use the thesaurus to find candidates, then take the candidate back to the dictionary to check that it fits. A thesaurus without a dictionary produces essays full of words that are almost right, which is worse than plain words that are exactly right.

Third, you want to know why candid means honest when it comes from a word for white. Open an *etymology dictionary*, in print or online. It traces the word's history: white, then pure, then unstained by dishonesty, then frank. It also shows relatives: candidate, because Roman office seekers wore white togas, and candle, because of the bright flame. This is the tool for remembering and connecting, and for reading old texts.

Which one to open? Meeting a word: dictionary. Choosing a word: thesaurus, then dictionary. Remembering or connecting a word: etymology dictionary. A search engine can lead you to all three, but read the entry, not just the first line a website shows you. The first line is often the most common meaning, which may not be the one in your sentence.

words.d: a reference that gives a word's spelling, pronunciation, part of speech, meanings and often its origin
a reference that lists words with similar or related meanings
a reference that traces the origin and history of words
honest and direct; not hiding your real opinion

look.title: Which Tool Would You Open?
look.text: A. You read the word sanguine in a history book and have no idea what it means. B. Your essay uses important five times. C. You want to know why the word salary has anything to do with salt. D. You are not sure whether affect or effect fits your sentence.
look.prompt: For each situation, name the tool you would open first, and say what you would do with the result before you trusted it.

check.q: Which tool should a writer open first to replace an overused word?
choices: A thesaurus, then a dictionary to check the choice
check.why: The thesaurus supplies candidates; the dictionary confirms which one fits the sentence.

check.q: What information does a standard dictionary entry usually include?
choices: Spelling, pronunciation, part of speech, meanings and often an origin
The word's translations into other languages
check.why: A dictionary entry answers what a word means and how it is used, and often gives its origin in brackets.

check.q: Why is a thesaurus risky when used by itself?
choices: It lists words that are almost right without explaining the differences
check.why: Muttered and declared appear together, but they mean different things; the dictionary sorts that out.

lessons.title: Building Your Own Word List
lessons.mainIdea: A personal word list works when each entry holds the word, its meaning in your words, a sentence and a hook to remember it.
reading: Most students who try to keep a vocabulary list quit within a week. The list becomes a graveyard of words copied from a glossary, never looked at again. The list that works is different in three ways. It is small, because you add only words you expect to meet again. It is yours, because the definition is in your own words. And it has a hook, a picture, story or root that makes each word stick.

Here is one entry, the way it should look. Word: reticent. Where I found it: the chapter on context clues. Meaning in my words: keeps quiet, does not share much. My sentence: My cousin is reticent at family dinners but loud online. Hook: sounds like reluctant, and a reticent person is reluctant to talk. Five lines. The whole thing took two minutes. A month from now, the sentence and the hook will bring the word back.

Where do the words come from? Bold words in textbooks. Words you had to guess from context in a novel. Words a teacher used twice in one class. Words on a quiz you got wrong. Cognates that surprised you. Do not add a word because it sounds impressive. Add it because you want to own it. Ten well-chosen words a week, kept for a school year, is more than three hundred words that are truly yours.

Review the list on purpose. Cover the meaning and try to say it. Use one of the words in an essay or a text message on purpose. Sort them by root, and you will start to see families. The point was never the list. The point is that the next time a chemistry quiz asks about a centrifuge, or a poem uses a word like *candid*, you are not a stranger to it. You have been introduced.

words.d: an alphabetical list of terms and their meanings, usually at the back of a book
a picture, story, root or sound-alike that helps you remember a word
honest and direct; not hiding your real opinion

look.title: One Entry From a Word List
look.text: Word: benevolent. Found in: history reading about a charity. Meaning in my words: wanting to do good for others. My sentence: The benevolent neighbor shoveled every sidewalk on the block. Hook: bene means good, like benefit, and volent is like volunteer, someone who wills to help.

check.q: What makes a personal word list work, according to the lesson?
choices: Adding at least fifty words a week
Keeping it small, in your own words, with a hook for each entry
check.why: A short list of chosen words, defined your own way, with a memory hook, is the one students keep using.

check.q: Which of these is a hook in the sense the lesson means?
choices: The page number where a word appears
Noticing that reticent sounds like reluctant
check.why: A hook is a sound-alike, root, picture or story that helps the word stick in memory.

check.q: What does the lesson say about words that merely sound impressive?
choices: Add them only if they are Latin
Add them in a separate list
Do not add them unless you want to own them
check.why: The list is for words you expect to meet and use, not for decoration.

review.why: The thesaurus supplies options; the dictionary confirms connotation so the word fits exactly.

chapters.title: Figurative Language
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a writer say one thing and mean another, and how do readers know when it is happening?

story.title: Two Men, a Wall and a Question
story.kicker: Robert Frost's poem about repairing a stone wall seems to be about stones, until the reader notices what the stones stand for.
paragraphs: Every spring in northern New England, the ground thaws and the old stone walls between farms tumble a little. Frost heaves the stones. Hunters knock them loose. In 1914 Robert Frost published a poem called Mending Wall about two neighbors who walk the line between their farms each spring, each picking up the fallen stones on his own side and setting them back. For the first several lines, that is all that happens. Stones, hands, a walk.

The poem opens with a line that sounds like a riddle: Something there is that doesn't love a wall. The speaker does not say what the something is. Cold weather, maybe. Or something in nature that dislikes barriers. As he works, he starts to tease his neighbor. There are no cows here to keep in or out, he points out. His apple trees will never cross over and eat the neighbor's pine cones. Why do they need a wall at all?

The neighbor has one answer, and he gives it twice: Good fences make good neighbors. He does not explain. He learned it from his father, and he will not think past it. The speaker watches him carry a stone in each hand and imagines him as an old-stone savage armed, a man from a darker age moving in darkness. That is not a description of a farmer. It is a picture of a mind that has closed.

By the end, a reader realizes the poem was never only about a wall. The wall is a wall, but it is also every barrier people keep up out of habit. The neighbor's saying is a saying, but it is also the way an old idea can keep a person from thinking. And the speaker, who wants the wall gone, still shows up every spring to help rebuild it. The poem does not tell you who is right. It hands you the stones.

This is what figurative language does. It lets a plain thing, a wall, a road, a bird, carry a second weight of meaning without ever announcing it. Frost was a master of it, but the same move happens in speeches, song lyrics, ads and the way your friend says she is drowning in homework. This chapter is about noticing the second weight, naming it and saying what it does.
story.think: The speaker mocks the wall but helps rebuild it every year. What might Frost be suggesting about people who criticize a habit and keep it anyway?

lessons.title: Metaphor and Simile, Closer Up
lessons.mainIdea: A metaphor has two parts, the thing meant and the image used, and the meaning lives in what the two share.
reading: Juliet is the sun. Romeo says so when he sees her at a window: It is the east, and Juliet is the sun. Nobody thinks Juliet is a ball of burning gas. Romeo means that she lights his world, that everything else looks dim next to her, that his day begins when she appears. He has taken one thing, Juliet, and spoken of it as though it were another thing, the sun. That is a *metaphor*. A simile does the same thing but announces the comparison with like or as: her smile was like sunrise.

Every metaphor has two halves. The thing actually being talked about is the *tenor*, here Juliet. The image borrowed to describe it is the *vehicle*, here the sun. The meaning is whatever the two share: brightness, warmth, being the center of things. To read a metaphor, name both halves and then ask what they have in common. Not everything. The sun is also hot enough to burn and impossible to look at. Romeo is not saying that. Context tells you which shared traits count.

Metaphors hide in ordinary speech. Time is money. She has a heart of stone. He shot down my idea. The deadline is looming. We do not notice these because they are worn smooth. But even the worn ones shape thinking. If time is money, then time can be wasted, spent, saved and budgeted, and you will feel that a lazy afternoon is a loss. Notice the vehicle, and you notice the attitude riding inside it.

In your own writing, a fresh metaphor is worth ten adjectives. Instead of the hallway was very crowded and loud, try the hallway was a river at flood. The reader gets crowding, motion, noise and danger in six words. Just keep the vehicle consistent. If the hallway is a river, do not have students marching through it two sentences later. A river does not march.

words.d: a figure of speech that speaks of one thing as if it were another, without like or as
in a metaphor, the actual subject being described
in a metaphor, the image borrowed to describe the subject
a comparison that uses like or as

look.title: Romeo at the Window
look.text: But, soft! what light through yonder window breaks? / It is the east, and Juliet is the sun.
look.cite: William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet, Act 2, about 1595
look.prompt: Name the tenor and the vehicle. List two traits of the sun Romeo means and one trait he does not mean, and say how you can tell.

check.q: In Juliet is the sun, what is the vehicle?
check.why: The vehicle is the borrowed image, the sun; Juliet is the tenor.

check.q: How does a simile differ from a metaphor?
choices: A simile announces the comparison with like or as
check.why: Her smile was like sunrise is a simile; her smile was sunrise is a metaphor.

check.q: What is wrong with the hallway was a river, and students marched through it?
choices: The vehicle is inconsistent; a river does not march
check.why: Once the hallway is a river, the action should fit a river: students should flow or be swept.

lessons.title: Extended Metaphor and Conceit
lessons.mainIdea: When a writer keeps one comparison going through a whole poem or passage, every line adds a new point of contact.
reading: Emily Dickinson begins a poem, Hope is the thing with feathers, that perches in the soul. That alone is a metaphor: hope is a bird. But she does not stop. The bird sings a tune without words. It never stops singing. It sings sweetest in the storm. It has kept her warm in the coldest land, and it has never asked her for a crumb. Each line finds one more way a bird and hope are alike. A comparison carried through many lines is an *extended metaphor*.

Reading an extended metaphor means tracking the points of contact. Make two columns: bird on one side, hope on the other. Perches: hope settles in and stays. Sings without words: hope does not need reasons. Sings in the storm: hope is strongest in trouble. Never asks for a crumb: hope costs nothing. When you have the columns, you have the poem. Shakespeare does the same when a character says all the world's a stage and all the men and women merely players, then runs through the seven ages of a life as if they were scenes.

A *conceit* is an extended metaphor that is surprising or far-fetched, joining two things that seem to have nothing in common and making it work anyway. The poet John Donne, writing around 1600, compared two lovers who must part to the two legs of a drawing compass. One leg stays fixed at the center while the other travels in a circle, leaning toward the first, and the fixed leg's steadiness is what makes the circle come out true. A compass is a strange way to talk about love. That strangeness is the point. It forces the reader to think.

Extended metaphors also live outside poetry. A coach calls the season a war and then talks about battles, soldiers and casualties. A politician calls the economy a ship and then speaks of steering, storms and staying the course. Once you spot the vehicle, ask what it makes you feel and what it leaves out. If the economy is a ship, there is one captain. Someone who wants you to trust one leader might like that image very much.

words.d: a single comparison developed over several lines or a whole passage
an extended metaphor that joins two very unlike things in a surprising, clever way
here, a drawing tool with two hinged legs used to make circles

look.title: Hope as a Bird
look.text: Hope is the thing with feathers / That perches in the soul, / And sings the tune without the words, / And never stops at all,
look.cite: Emily Dickinson, poem written about 1861, published 1891
look.prompt: Make the two-column chart for these four lines: what the bird does on one side, what that says about hope on the other. Which line surprised you most?

check.q: What makes a metaphor extended?
choices: It is carried through several lines, adding new points of contact
check.why: Dickinson's bird keeps gaining traits across the poem: perching, singing, never asking for a crumb.

check.q: What distinguishes a conceit from an ordinary extended metaphor?
choices: It joins two things so unlike that the comparison surprises the reader
check.why: Donne's lovers as compass legs is far-fetched on purpose; the strangeness makes the reader think.

check.q: Why should a reader be alert when a politician calls the economy a ship?
choices: Because the metaphor is always false
Because it proves the speaker is lying
Because the vehicle implies one captain and may steer the listener toward trusting one leader
check.why: Every vehicle carries hidden attitudes; a ship suggests a single hand on the wheel.

lessons.title: Symbols
lessons.mainIdea: A symbol is a real thing in a text that also stands for an idea, and you know it is a symbol because the text keeps returning to it.
reading: In Mending Wall, the wall is a real wall. Stones fall, the men lift them. But the poem keeps circling back to it, arguing about it, asking what it is for. A thing that is fully itself and also stands for something larger is a *symbol*. The wall stands for the barriers people keep up out of habit. A metaphor says A is B. A symbol just shows you A, over and over, until you feel B standing behind it.

Some symbols are shared by a whole culture. A dove for peace, a red rose for love, a skull for death, a scale for justice, a flag for a nation. You do not need a footnote for these. Others belong to one work only. In Paul Laurence Dunbar's 1896 poem We Wear the Mask, the mask is not a real object. It is the smile Black Americans were forced to wear over pain, the poem says, and the whole poem is the mask being described. The reader learns what it means by reading, not by knowing in advance.

How do you tell a symbol from a mere object? Three tests. Repetition: does the text mention it more than once, especially at important moments? Emphasis: does it appear in the title, the first line or the last? Weight: do characters treat it as more than it is, arguing over it, protecting it, longing for it? A doorknob mentioned once is a doorknob. A locked door the whole story keeps returning to is probably more.

One warning. Students sometimes turn every object into a symbol. The blue curtains mean the author is sad. Usually the blue curtains mean the room had blue curtains. A symbol earns its meaning by the way the text uses it. If you claim something is a symbol, you should be able to point to the repetitions and the moments that gave it weight. If you cannot, let the curtains be curtains.

words.d: a concrete thing in a text that also stands for a larger idea
special stress or importance given to something, such as by placing it first or last
meaning exactly what the words say, with no second meaning

look.title: The Mask
look.text: We wear the mask that grins and lies, / It hides our cheeks and shades our eyes,
look.cite: Paul Laurence Dunbar, We Wear the Mask, 1896
look.prompt: The mask grins, lies, hides and shades. What does it stand for, and who is the we? Which of the three tests for a symbol does the title alone already pass?

check.q: How does a symbol differ from a metaphor?
choices: A symbol uses like or as
A symbol is a real thing in the text that also carries a larger meaning, without saying A is B
A symbol appears only in poetry
A symbol is always an animal
check.why: The wall in Mending Wall is a real wall that also stands for barriers; nobody says the wall is a habit.

check.q: Which is a test for whether an object is a symbol?
choices: Whether the text returns to it at important moments
Whether it is mentioned exactly once
check.why: Repetition, emphasis and weight are the three tests; a thing mentioned once is usually just a thing.

check.q: What does the lesson say about the blue curtains?
choices: They usually just mean the room had blue curtains, unless the text gives them weight
They are a shared cultural symbol
check.why: A symbol must earn its meaning through the text's use of it, not through a reader's guess.

lessons.title: Allegory: The Whole Story Stands for Something
lessons.mainIdea: An allegory is a story in which the characters and events line up point by point with a second meaning outside the story.
reading: Imagine a story about a farm where the animals drive out the farmer and run the place themselves. The pigs take charge. They promise equality, then slowly take the farmer's privileges for themselves until nobody can tell pig from man. George Orwell published that story, Animal Farm, in 1945, and every reader knew that the farm was Russia after its revolution and the pigs were the leaders who betrayed it. A story whose characters and events stand, one for one, for something outside the story is an *allegory*.

An allegory is a symbol stretched over a whole narrative. In a symbol, one object carries a second meaning. In an allegory, the whole cast does. John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress, from 1678, follows a man named Christian who leaves the City of Destruction and walks toward the Celestial City, passing through the Slough of Despond and Vanity Fair. The names give it away. Despond means hopelessness. Vanity means empty pride. The journey is a soul's life, and every stop is a temptation or a trial.

The ancient Greek philosopher Plato told an allegory about prisoners chained in a cave, able to see only shadows on the wall. One escapes, sees the sun and the real world, and returns to tell the others, who do not believe him. The cave is ignorance. The shadows are appearances mistaken for truth. The sun is knowledge. Plato used the story because an argument about knowledge is hard to follow, and a story about a cave is not.

To read an allegory, build the key. Write the story element on one side and its outside meaning on the other: pigs, leaders; cave, ignorance. Then ask what the story lets the writer say that a plain statement could not. Orwell could show betrayal happening step by step. Bunyan could make a life of faith into a road with a map. Allegory turns an idea into something you can watch.

words.d: a story whose characters and events each stand for something outside the story, forming a second meaning
to lose hope; the Slough of Despond in Bunyan's allegory is a swamp of hopelessness
empty pride in appearance or possessions

look.title: Build the Key
look.text: A short film shows a classroom where one student keeps the light switch. When she leaves, students argue about who should hold it. Some want to take turns. A few form a group and lock the switch in a box, then charge the others for light.
look.prompt: Make a two-column key for this allegory: what does the switch stand for, and the students who lock it away? What point does the story make that a speech could not make as well?

check.q: What is the difference between a symbol and an allegory?
choices: A symbol is a single object with a second meaning; an allegory is a whole story whose parts line up with a second meaning
An allegory uses like or as
check.why: Allegory is a symbol stretched over an entire narrative, character by character.

check.q: In Plato's cave, what do the shadows represent?
check.why: The prisoners believe the shadows are real, which stands for mistaking appearance for truth.

check.q: Why do writers use allegory instead of stating an idea plainly?
choices: Because allegories are easier to write
Because ideas cannot be stated plainly
Because a story lets readers watch an idea unfold step by step
check.why: Orwell could show a betrayal happening; a plain statement can only name it.

lessons.title: Three Kinds of Irony
lessons.mainIdea: Irony is a gap between what is said or expected and what is true, and it comes in verbal, situational and dramatic forms.
reading: It is pouring rain, and your friend says, Great weather for a picnic. She means the opposite of what she says, and she expects you to know it. That is *verbal irony*, saying one thing to mean another. When it is meant to sting, it is sarcasm. Verbal irony works only if the listener catches the gap. Tone of voice, context and a shared sense of how things are all help. In writing, where there is no tone of voice, the context has to do the whole job.

*Situational irony* is a gap between what is expected and what happens. A fire station burns down. A lifeguard drowns. In O. Henry's 1905 story The Gift of the Magi, a young wife sells her long hair to buy a chain for her husband's watch. He, the same day, sells the watch to buy combs for her hair. Each gift is now useless, and each is perfect. Nobody said the opposite of what they meant; the situation itself turned inside out.

*Dramatic irony* is a gap between what a character knows and what the audience knows. At the end of Romeo and Juliet, Romeo finds Juliet in the tomb and believes she is dead. The audience knows she has only taken a sleeping potion and will wake in minutes. We want to shout at him. That helplessness, watching a character act on a mistake we can see and he cannot, is the feeling dramatic irony creates. Horror films use it constantly: the audience knows what is behind the door.

To name the irony in a text, first find the gap. Between words and meaning: verbal. Between expectation and outcome: situational. Between a character's knowledge and the audience's: dramatic. Then ask what the gap does. Verbal irony often makes a speaker sound sharp or amused. Situational irony makes a story feel like fate or a joke. Dramatic irony makes an audience tense or sad. Irony is never just decoration. It always shifts how the reader feels.

words.d: saying one thing while meaning the opposite, expecting the listener to notice
a gap between what is expected to happen and what actually happens
a gap between what a character knows and what the audience knows
verbal irony meant to mock or wound

look.title: Sort the Three
look.text: A. A character hides in the one closet the audience just saw the villain enter. B. A student who wrote an essay against cell phones in class wins a phone as the prize. C. Someone spills soup on her shirt and says, Smooth move.
look.prompt: Label each situation verbal, situational or dramatic irony and explain the gap in each. Which one would make you laugh, and which would make you tense?

check.q: Which is an example of situational irony?
choices: A character says nice job after a teammate drops the ball
The audience knows the letter never arrived, but the hero does not
A poem compares hope to a bird
check.why: A fire station is expected to prevent fires; its burning is a gap between expectation and outcome.

check.q: What creates dramatic irony in the tomb scene of Romeo and Juliet?
choices: Romeo says the opposite of what he means
The audience knows Juliet is alive, and Romeo does not
Juliet expected Romeo and he did not come
check.why: The gap is between the character's knowledge and the audience's.

check.q: Why does verbal irony in writing depend so heavily on context?
choices: Because written irony is illegal in essays
Because irony only works in poems
Because there is no tone of voice on the page to signal the gap
check.why: In speech, tone shows the gap; in writing, the surrounding words must do that work.

lessons.title: Paradox and Oxymoron
lessons.mainIdea: A paradox seems to contradict itself but holds a truth, and an oxymoron packs that contradiction into two words.
reading: In Hamlet, the prince says, I must be cruel only to be kind. On its face that makes no sense. Cruelty is the opposite of kindness. But Hamlet means that harsh words now may save his mother from a worse fate later, the way a doctor may hurt you to heal you. A statement that seems to contradict itself and yet turns out to be true is a *paradox*. The reader's job is to find the sense hidden inside the contradiction.

Paradoxes appear wherever a writer wants to stop you cold. The witches in Macbeth chant, Fair is foul, and foul is fair, and the whole play proves them right: what looks good turns out evil, and evil wears a fair face. Everyday speech has them too. Less is more. You have to spend money to make money. The only constant is change. Each one forces you to pause and work out how both halves can hold.

An *oxymoron* is a paradox shrunk to a phrase, usually two words that fight each other. Deafening silence. Jumbo shrimp. Bittersweet. Living dead. Juliet says parting is such sweet sorrow, and the sweet and the sorrow are both true: it hurts to leave, and it is sweet because she will see him again. The oxymoron does in two words what a paragraph of explanation might do, and it does it with a jolt.

When you meet a paradox or an oxymoron, do not dismiss it as nonsense. Ask under what conditions both halves can be true. Deafening silence: silence so complete that it feels like a pressure on the ears. Cruel to be kind: cruel now, kind in the long run. The figure is a small puzzle, and solving it is often the moment the writer's meaning opens up. If it cannot be solved, then the writer may simply have made an error, but that is rare in good writing.

words.d: a statement that seems to contradict itself but contains a truth
a figure of speech that joins two contradictory words, such as deafening silence
to state the opposite of something; to be in conflict with it

look.title: Hamlet's Puzzle
look.text: I must be cruel, only to be kind.
look.prompt: Under what conditions can cruelty and kindness both be true at once? Give an example from ordinary life, such as a coach, a parent or a doctor, that fits the line.

check.q: What is a paradox?
choices: A statement that seems self-contradictory but holds a truth
A comparison using like or as
A word that means its opposite
A story with a hidden meaning
check.why: Cruel to be kind seems impossible until you see cruelty now can produce kindness later.

check.q: Which phrase is an oxymoron?
check.why: Deafening and silence contradict each other in a single two-word phrase.

check.q: What should a reader do when a statement seems to contradict itself?
choices: Assume the writer made an error
Ask under what conditions both halves could be true
check.why: Solving the small puzzle is usually the moment the writer's meaning opens.

lessons.title: Allusion and How to Look One Up
lessons.mainIdea: An allusion borrows a famous story in a few words, and a reader who does not know the story can find it in a minute.
reading: In 1858, Abraham Lincoln opened a speech about slavery with the words, A house divided against itself cannot stand. He did not invent the line. It comes from the Gospel of Mark, and his listeners knew it. By borrowing it, Lincoln made the nation into a house and let the Bible's authority stand behind his warning without arguing for it. A brief reference to a well-known story, person, place or text is an *allusion*. It works by trust: the writer trusts you to know the reference.

Allusions come from a few big sources. Biblical: a good Samaritan is a stranger who helps; a David against a Goliath is a small fighter against a giant; a prodigal son is a wanderer who comes home. Classical, from Greek and Roman myth: an Achilles heel is one fatal weakness; a Pandora's box is a source of troubles better left shut; a Trojan horse is a gift hiding an attack; a task like Sisyphus's never ends. Historical: to meet your Waterloo is to suffer your final defeat, after the battle where Napoleon lost in 1815. Literary: a Scrooge is a miser, from Dickens.

The problem is that nobody knows every story, and writers do not stop to explain. So learn to look one up fast. Take the odd phrase, the name or the place you do not recognize, and search it with the word meaning or origin. Read a source you trust, an encyclopedia or a dictionary of allusions, not the first comment thread. Then go back to the sentence and ask what the story adds. Usually it adds a whole plot in three words.

Allusions also appear in songs, films and titles. A team called the Titans alludes to giants of Greek myth. A headline about a modern Trojan horse is warning about a hidden threat. Once you start noticing, you will find that much of what you read is quietly quoting something older. Knowing the source is like getting the joke that everyone else was already laughing at.

words.d: a brief reference to a well-known story, person, place or text that the reader is expected to recognize
a single weak spot in someone otherwise strong, from the Greek hero who could be wounded only in the heel
a final, crushing defeat, from the 1815 battle Napoleon lost

look.title: Lincoln Borrows a Line
look.text: A house divided against itself cannot stand.
look.cite: Abraham Lincoln, speech at Springfield, Illinois, June 16, 1858, quoting the Gospel of Mark
look.prompt: What is the house in Lincoln's speech, and what divides it? Why might a borrowed line carry more force than an original one in this case?

check.q: What is an allusion?
choices: A brief reference to a well-known story or text the reader is expected to know
A comparison using like or as
A softer word for a harsh thing
check.why: Lincoln's house divided borrowed a Bible verse his audience recognized.

check.q: What does it mean to call a problem someone's Achilles heel?
check.why: Achilles could be wounded only in the heel, so the phrase names a single weak spot.

check.q: What is the best way to look up an unfamiliar allusion?
choices: Search the phrase with meaning or origin and read a trusted reference
Skip it, since allusions rarely matter
Look it up in a thesaurus
check.why: A quick search of the phrase plus a reliable source recovers the story in a minute.

lessons.title: Euphemism: The Softer Word
lessons.mainIdea: A euphemism replaces a blunt word with a gentler one, and readers should ask whether it is kindness or a way to hide the truth.
reading: Nobody at a funeral says the person died. They say she passed away, she is gone, we lost her. A company does not fire two hundred workers; it lets them go, or downsizes, or restructures. A used car is pre-owned. A lie is a misstatement. Each of these is a *euphemism*, a mild or indirect word put in place of one that is harsh, embarrassing or frightening. The word comes from Greek parts meaning good speech.

Some euphemisms are simple kindness. Passed away lets a grieving family avoid a blunt word in a hard hour. Restroom spares everyone a description. Nobody is fooled and nobody is harmed. But other euphemisms are built to fool. When a military report says collateral damage, it means civilians were killed. When a budget speaks of revenue enhancements, it means taxes went up. The soft word is there to keep you from feeling what the hard word would make you feel.

The test is simple. Translate the euphemism into the plainest word you can, and ask whether the writer wanted you to. If the plain word is died and the setting is a funeral, the euphemism is doing gentle work. If the plain word is killed and the setting is a report meant to reassure the public, the euphemism is doing dishonest work. Notice, too, that euphemisms tend to be longer and vaguer than the words they replace. Extra syllables are often extra distance from the truth.

As a writer, use euphemism on purpose and rarely. In a note to a grieving friend, passed away is right. In an analysis of a company's decision, write that it fired workers, because that is what happened. And when you catch a euphemism in a speech, an ad or a news release, name it in your writing. Saying that a speaker called layoffs a restructuring is itself a sharp piece of analysis.

a military euphemism for civilians killed or property destroyed unintentionally
plain and direct, without softening

choices: A mild or indirect word used in place of a harsh one
A reference to a famous story
A comparison between two unlike things
check.why: Passed away for died and let go for fired are euphemisms.

check.q: When is a euphemism most likely dishonest, according to the lesson?
choices: When it is used at a funeral
When it is shorter than the plain word
When it keeps the public from feeling what the plain word would reveal
check.why: Collateral damage for civilian deaths exists to blunt the reader's reaction to a hard fact.

choices: Check whether it appears in a dictionary
